soil-class-138.title: Podzol, the ash-grey soil beneath northern forests
soil-class-138.text: Peasants breaking such soils for the first time ploughed up what looked like a layer of ash. Dokuchaev named the soil for it in 1875: podzol is Russian for 'under-ash'. A Podzol is an acid soil with an organic topsoil over a bleached, ash-grey leached layer and a subsoil enriched in iron, aluminum or humus. It is the typical soil of boreal and coniferous forests, and of the eucalypt forests and heathlands of southern Australia too. Under 5 to 10 cm of decomposing litter lies an E horizon, usually 4 to 8 cm thick and poor in iron and aluminum oxides and humus. Below it sits a red or red-brown podzolic B horizon. {{ref:soil-form-061}} builds this profile. Dissolved organic matter binds iron and aluminum into chelates, and percolating water carries them from the E to the B horizon. Sometimes they cement a hardpan called ortstein. Podzols form mostly on quartz-rich sands, sandstone or debris of magmatic rock under high rainfall. In cool humid climates decay is slow, so acid layers of litter called mor build up. Most Podzols make poor farmland: sandy, short of water and nutrients, acidic, low in phosphate and toxic with aluminum. Grazing suits them best, though limed and fertilized loamy types can crop well. They cover about 4,850,000 square kilometers, mostly in the temperate and boreal Northern Hemisphere. Other systems give them other names. USDA and Chinese taxonomy say Spodosols, Canada has its Podzolic order, Australia uses Podosols and Brazil Espodossolos.

soil-class-123.title: Chernozem, the black earth of the steppes
soil-class-123.text: Some of the richest farmland on Earth goes by a plain name: black earth. Chernozem joins the Russian words for 'black' and 'earth', and the soil is also called regur. It holds 4% to 16% humus, with plenty of phosphorus and ammonia compounds. In the WRB key a Chernozem has a very dark, well-structured topsoil and secondary carbonates, lime deposited within the soil itself. That dark layer runs from a few centimeters to 1.5 meters (60 inches) thick in Ukraine and the Red River Valley. Chernozem covers about 230 million hectares in two belts. One is the Eurasian Steppe. The other runs from the Canadian Prairies south through the Great Plains to Kansas. Dokuchaev studied the steppe soils of Poltava in 1883. That year he published {{ref:soil-hist-002}}, the first description of the soil in European Russia. The soil is very fertile and holds much moisture. Long cropping still needs fertilizer, because its humus, and the nutrients that come with it, steadily declines. Its value has even fed a black market. Ukraine banned farmland sales from 1992 to 2020, but soil trucked away could be sold. In 2011 that trade was put at about US$900 million a year. In the WRB the USDA Mollisols split three ways: Chernozems, {{ref:soil-class-130}} and {{ref:soil-class-135}}. Together they match Canada's Chernozemic order.

soil-class-142.title: Solonchak, where salt builds up in the soil
soil-class-142.text: Solonchak is Russian for 'salt marsh', from sol, 'salt'. In the WRB it names a group of pale or grey, poorly drained soils of arid to subhumid lands that hold high concentrations of soluble salts. Its neighbors say a lot about it. Many lime-rich soils, the {{ref:soil-class-121}}, lie next to Solonchaks that are really salt-affected members of that same group. Solonchaks also turn up beside {{ref:soil-class-143}} soils, along with {{ref:soil-class-127}} and {{ref:soil-class-130}}. Crossing to the U.S. system shows the same family resemblance. Most USDA Aridisols fall into just four WRB groups: Solonchaks, the lime-rich soils above, and the soils rich in gypsum or silica described in {{ref:soil-class-129}} and {{ref:soil-class-125}}. People can make Solonchaks too. Irrigation with saline groundwater has caused catastrophic salinization and Solonchak formation, as in Central Asia. Water meant to grow crops left salt behind instead.

soil-class-143.title: Solonetz, the soil with a sodium-laden subsoil
soil-class-143.text: Many Ukrainian villages carry the folk word solontsi, meaning salty soil. The WRB name Solonetz comes from the same Russian root, sol, 'salt'. A Solonetz has a clay-enriched subsoil high in exchangeable sodium within the upper 100 cm. That layer is the natric horizon, named from Latin natrium, 'sodium'. It holds more clay than the layer above, and over 15% of its exchange sites carry sodium, a share measured as the {{ref:soil-chem-018}}. Solonetz zones go with Solonchaks, {{ref:soil-class-127}} and {{ref:soil-class-130}}. In USDA soil taxonomy Solonetz are sodium-rich Alfisols, and any Alfisol or Mollisol with a natric horizon keys out as Solonetz. Canada's soils show how such a soil ages. Starting from saline parent material, it develops into Solonetz, then Solodized Solonetz, then Solod, as leaching removes the salts. In the end the sodic B horizon may disintegrate. The name has deep roots in the science. Solonetz is one of the Russian soil terms, with chernozem, podzol and gley, that Dokuchaev's work brought into international use.

soil-class-120.title: Anthrosols, soils remade by centuries of farming
soil-class-120.text: Some soils carry a human signature. Anthrosols are soils formed or heavily changed by long-term human use, such as irrigation, added organic waste or paddy-field cultivation. They can form from any parent soil and are common where people have farmed for centuries. The clues are distinctive: high phosphate from bones, tissue or excrement, dark color, high pH from added wood ash, and buried tools or waste. A qualifier in the name records the cause. Plaggic means long manuring, irragric flooding or watering over the surface, hortic deep cultivation and kitchen waste, and anthraquic man-made water management such as terracing. In north-western Europe they commonly have plaggic or terric horizons built up with manure, together covering some 500,000 hectares. Rich in minerals and decayed organic matter, Anthrosols are good for farming, and well-managed ones store carbon. Archaeologists use them too. Spotted by eye or even from satellite images, they mark sites of long-term habitation. Similar soils carry many national names, among them {{ref:soil-class-149}}, paddy soils, the Amazon's {{ref:soil-class-053}}, Agrozems in Russia and Anthroposols in Australia and Canada. That variety raises a real question. Because Anthrosols differ so widely in composition and structure, soil scientists debate whether they should be an independent soil group at all.

soil-class-148.title: Aridity, the drying of the land
soil-class-148.text: Arid areas make up about 43% of the world's land. Aridity is the condition of regions with low annual precipitation, high temperatures and little available water, and such regions tend to have degraded soils. Where it falls depends mainly on the general circulation of the atmosphere, which shifts with climate change. Land-use change can also raise the demand on soil water. A December 2024 UNCCD report found that over three-quarters of Earth's land has become permanently drier in recent decades. A quarter of people live in dry regions that keep expanding. Warming-driven aridity also adds to the salinization of waterlogged soils.

soil-class-127.title: Gleysols, soils stained by groundwater
soil-class-127.text: Break open a clod from a Gleysol and its inside is grey or blue, while its outer faces are rusty. These gleyic colors mark a soil saturated by groundwater long enough, unless drained, to change its iron. Gleysols are also called meadow soils, groundwater soils or Gleyzems. The WRB draws a sharp line by the source of the water. Redox features from rising groundwater make a Gleysol; those from stagnant surface water make a {{ref:soil-class-144}} or a {{ref:soil-class-136}}. Gleysols form in many unconsolidated sediments, mostly river, marine and lake deposits, in depressions and low positions with shallow groundwater. They cover an estimated 720 million hectares and occur in nearly all climates. They are most extensive in northern Russia, Siberia, Canada, Alaska, China and Bangladesh. About 200 million hectares lie in the tropics, mainly in the Amazon, equatorial Africa and the coastal swamps of Southeast Asia. Drained, they carry arable crops, dairy farming and horticulture, and in the tropics and subtropics they are widely planted with rice. They also hold an unusual mineral. Green rust, a layered iron(II)-iron(III) hydroxide, occurs in them as fougerite. In USDA soil taxonomy they match the Aqu- suborders of Entisols, Inceptisols and Mollisols.

soil-class-126.title: Fluvisols, the young layered soils of floodplains
soil-class-126.text: In prehistoric times people already prized these soils, for their natural fertility and for dry living sites on river levees. Fluvisols are genetically young, stratified soils in river, lake or marine sediments. They show clear layering and weak horizons, and under natural conditions they flood from time to time. They occur on alluvial plains, river fans, valleys and tidal marshes on every continent and in every climate zone. Large areas lie along the Amazon, the Ganges plain and Lake Chad, and in deltas such as the Mekong, Mississippi and Nile. With water control, many dryland crops grow on them. Paddy rice is widespread on irrigated and drained tropical Fluvisols. The coast is harder ground. Coastal Fluvisols with sulfidic material are acid sulfate soils, limited by low pH, toxic aluminum and salt. Strongly saline tidal land is best left under mangroves. In USDA soil taxonomy Fluvisols correspond to the fluvents and fluvaquents.

soil-class-117.title: Acrisols, weathered tropical soils ruled by aluminum
soil-class-117.text: Around the Amazon's fertile patches of {{ref:soil-class-053}} lies a 'common soil', and most of it is infertile Acrisol. Acrisols are strongly weathered soils with low-activity clays, clays with a low cation exchange capacity. In them exchangeable aluminum exceeds the exchangeable base cations. They go with humid tropical and subtropical climates, such as Brazil's, and often carry forest. Low fertility and toxic aluminum limit farming. Many Acrisols therefore serve for forestry, low-intensity pasture or protected areas. Where climate allows, tea, rubber, oil palm, coffee and sugar cane can be grown on them. In USDA soil taxonomy they match the Humult, Udult and Ustult suborders of the Ultisols, plus Oxisols with a kandic horizon and some Alfisols. Going the other way, most Ultisols are classed in the WRB as either Acrisols or {{ref:soil-class-118}}.

soil-class-131.title: Leptosols, thin soils from the tropics to the peaks
soil-class-131.text: Leptosols cover about 1.7 billion hectares, from the tropics to polar regions and from sea level to the highest peaks. They are very shallow soils over continuous rock, or deeper soils packed with gravel and stones. Mountains hold many of them, notably in Asia, South America, northern Canada and Alaska, and so do the Saharan and Arabian deserts. Elsewhere they occur on hard rock, or where erosion has kept pace with soil formation or stripped the topsoil. The most extensive Leptosols on Earth are Lithic Leptosols in mountain regions, less than 10 cm deep. They hold little water, so they are poor for rainfed farming, though some suit tree crops or extensive grazing. Older names linger. The 1974 FAO legend called Leptosols on limestone {{ref:soil-class-050}} and those on acid rock Rankers. In the WRB such a limestone soil may key out as a Leptosol, Chernozem, {{ref:soil-class-130}} or {{ref:soil-class-135}}. In USDA terms many orthents, and shallow or gravelly Mollisols, belong to the Leptosols.

soil-class-122.title: Cambisols, soils just beginning to change
soil-class-122.text: Some of the most productive soils on earth are barely formed. Cambisols are moderately developed soils at the beginning of soil formation, shown by weak brownish color or structure in the profile. Temperate Cambisols rank among the most productive soils on earth, and most Cambisols make good, intensively used farmland. They form in medium- and fine-textured material from many rock types, mostly in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits. Worldwide they cover an estimated 15 million square kilometers. They are widespread in temperate and boreal lands glaciated in the Pleistocene. There the parent material is young and soil formation is slow. In the tropics they are less common, appearing mainly where active erosion keeps soils young. Europe's weakly leached soils known as {{ref:soil-class-048}} are Cambisols in the WRB. Poland's brown forest soils correspond to Cambisols and to USDA Udepts.

soil-class-133.title: Luvisols, fertile soils with clay washed downward
soil-class-133.text: Over time, water seeping down through a Luvisol moves clay from the upper soil into the layer beneath. The result defines the group: an argic horizon, a subsurface layer with more clay than the material above, formed as water washes clay downward. Where uneroded, a paler, clay-depleted eluvial horizon lies above it. The clays are little weathered, high-activity 2:1 types. They give a high cation exchange capacity and high base saturation, with base cations equal to or greater than exchangeable aluminum. Luvisols cover 500–600 million hectares, mainly in temperate zones. They form on many parent materials and are generally fertile and widely farmed. In Mediterranean regions hematite colors them red as Chromic Luvisols. Such soils with strong wet-dry seasons, of the kind described in {{ref:soil-class-063}}, are called calcic and chromic luvisols. In USDA soil taxonomy most Luvisols are Alfisols. Canada's system also has Luvisols, whose clay-enriched Bt horizon forms mainly by {{ref:soil-form-060}}.

soil-class-145.title: Technosols, the soils of cities, mines and dumps
soil-class-145.text: A landfill, a heap of mine spoil and a city pavement can all count as soil. Technosols are soils whose properties and formation are dominated by their technical, human-made origin. A Technosol holds a significant amount of artifacts, objects made by people, or has a geotechnical liner, or is sealed by technic hard material unlike natural rock. The group covers soils of landfills, sludge, cinders, mine spoil and ash, pavements with their underlying material, and constructed soils. Natural soil that has merely been transported does not count. Often called urban or mine soils, Technosols occur near cities, roads, mines, dumps, oil spills and fly-ash deposits, usually in small patches. They can change fast: a Technosol can differentiate A and O horizons at more than one centimeter per year. They are more likely than other soils to be contaminated, and many must be handled with care because of toxic industrial substances. Some are made on purpose to cover wastes such as mine tailings, as at Andacollo in Chile. Their closest relatives are {{ref:soil-class-120}}, soils created by long-term measures to raise fertility for farming.

soil-class-139.title: Regosols, the leftover group for barely formed soils
soil-class-139.text: Regosols are what remains when a soil fits no other group. They are very weakly developed mineral soils in unconsolidated material, with no significant profile development. Weak soils that qualify as Leptosols, Arenosols or Fluvisols are excluded. Their profiles stay minimal because they are young or form slowly. They cover about 260 million hectares, mainly in arid areas of the mid-western United States, northern Africa, the Near East and Australia. They are also extensive in eroding mountains. They match USDA Entisols and Australian Rudosols. Most are lightly grazed, some are irrigated intensively, and mountain Regosols are best left under forest.

soil-class-121.title: Calcisols, dryland soils rich in lime
soil-class-121.text: Some 10 million square kilometers may be Calcisols, almost all in the arid and semi-arid subtropics. These soils hold a substantial secondary accumulation of lime, calcium carbonate deposited within the soil. They are common on calcareous parent materials and widespread in arid and semi-arid lands, and older systems called them Desert soils and Takyrs. They develop mostly in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits of base-rich weathering material, on level to hilly land. Natural vegetation is sparse: drought-adapted shrubs and trees and short-lived grasses. Dryness, stoniness or a shallow petrocalcic horizon, a layer cemented by lime, limit farming. Yet irrigated, drained and fertilized Calcisols can be highly productive. Many occur alongside Solonchaks that are in fact salt-affected Calcisols. In the other direction, most USDA Aridisols fall into four WRB groups: Calcisols, Solonchaks, {{ref:soil-class-129}} and {{ref:soil-class-125}}.

soil-class-118.title: Alisols, acid soils with active clays
soil-class-118.text: Alisols pair lively clays with acid conditions. In these soils the clays are high-activity, yet exchangeable aluminum exceeds the exchangeable base cations. Their clay-enriched argic horizon has a high cation exchange capacity but low base saturation in the subsoil. Their clays are far more active than those of {{ref:soil-class-132}}, Acrisols and Ferralsols, and they tend to lie on younger or more geologically active terrain. They occur in tropical and humid subtropical climates and also in temperate regions. Farming them needs lime and fertilizer, and they erode easily. At their low pH, aluminum and manganese dissolve and can poison intolerant plants.

openers.world-reference-base-soil-groups: Travel from the northern forests to the tropics and the soil underfoot changes as much as the trees. Under boreal and coniferous forests lies an acid soil with a bleached, ash-grey layer below its organic topsoil. On the steppes a black earth holds 4% to 16% humus. Dry lands carry pale, salty soils, groundwater stains others grey or blue, and long human use, from irrigation to paddy fields, has remade some entirely. This chapter takes the reference soil groups of the World Reference Base one at a time, from very shallow soils over rock to strongly weathered tropical soils ruled by aluminum.
